Half Turn

GeometryCoordinatesInvariants
Game: Flip a little arrow around dots and watch where it lands; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the arrow ends or the blue dots, or focus one and press the arrow keys. Change the number of flips and tick the boxes to see names and guide lines.

Drag A, B or a blue center, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

The old Java applet flipped a red arrow in a row of points. The surprise is that after an even number of flips the arrow is only slid sideways, while after an odd number it is turned halfway around one particular point.

One flip about a point

A reflection in a point sends P to P′ so that O is the midpoint of PP′: SO(P) = 2O − P. Only O stays fixed, and doing the same flip twice gives SO2 = I. It is an isometry: distances and angles do not change, the orientation of a shape does not turn over, parallel lines stay parallel, and every line through O is carried back to itself.

Flip, flip, flip

Reflecting in O1, then O2, and so on up to On gives one map: p ↦ (−1)np + t, where t = 2(On − On−1 + … ± O1). For even n the sign is +1, so it is a translation by t. For odd n the sign is −1, so it is another half turn, this time about the point c = t/2 = On − On−1 + … + O1, which is a rotation through 180°. The logic test compared this with a second transcription of the applet's own Compute() on 200 configurations (20 seeds × 10 spinner values) and found no difference.

What the page gets wrong

The old page says: “For any n, AAn = BBn, AAn || BBn.” That is true only for even n, when AAn and BBn are both the translation vector t. For odd n, An = 2c − A and Bn = 2c − B, so the two segments are chords through c but usually have different lengths and directions. One worked case from the test: A=(230,120), B=(260,160), O1=(200,150), O2=(280,200), O3=(240,140). Then c=(160,90), A3=(90,60), B3=(60,20): AA3=(−140,−60) and BB3=(−200,−140) are neither equal nor parallel. The page's next sentence is right: both lines pass through c. Its formula SOSQ = −SQSO means the two orders give opposite translations by 2(O−Q) and 2(Q−O); the order matters unless O = Q.

What the applet offers

The spinner runs from 1 to 10 and starts at 3, not just “three or four” as the written page says; Show names and Show statement start unchecked. Those ranges and the red arrow with blue copies are kept here. Two deliberate presentation changes: the Java applet drops its centers at random, while this page uses a fixed seed (7) so a picture can be reproduced (press New centers for another set), and the handles stop at the board edge. The live cut-the-knot page has replaced the Java applet with a GeoGebra model; a 2010 capture of the same address on the Wayback Machine still shows the original <applet code="HalfTurn">.

Try 2 flips and drag one center: the whole final arrow slides by twice the drag. Then try 3 flips and tick Show statement: both long dashed lines meet at the same point.
